entrada.nota_de_retencion: el registro de decisiones (cierra la pregunta por el ciclo de vida de la corrida purgada): **no se persiste nada de un tercero**. aic:22270.texto: This casually posed and loosely rendered portrait originally made up part of the lower section, or predella, of an altarpiece for a church in Gambassi, near Florence. The images of the patron, Domenico, and his wife, Lucrezia, flanked additional, now-lost works. The painted strapwork around the portraits, discovered during recent conservation treatment, once formed part of a decorative pattern that would have extended throughout the predella; it indicates how all the individual paintings were interconnected. Andrea del Sarto added highlights at the bottom of each roundel, mimicking the natural light of the church, to create the illusion of the paintings being set within a three-dimensional frame.

cma:124091.texto: King Francis I’s deep interest in Italian Renaissance culture manifested itself not only through acquiring important works of art but also by bringing leading architects, scholars, and artists to Paris. Chief among these figures was the Florentine painter Andrea del Sarto. The sitter’s distinctively French hood and black veil suggest that someone talented closely connected to the artist painted this work during his brief time in France.

cma:146469.texto: Bronzino was court painter to Cosimo I de’Medici, the Duke of Florence. Though the woman cannot be definitively identified, she was likely affiliated with the Medici court. As in most of the portraits in this gallery, Bronzino emphasizes wealth, status, and courtly refinement above personality or individualized expression. The plain background further accentuates the work’s monumentality and grandeur, despite its small scale. The hand placed against the chest with elegantly spread fingers extends back to an ancient Greek pose of modesty, here emphasizing the proper comportment of a woman of high status. The sitter wears a linen partlet (collar) delicately embroidered in matt stitch, part of which is, like her cuffs, trimmed in fine lace.
cma:146469.title: Portrait of a Woman

cma:153406.texto: Sebastian, a bodyguard for the ancient Roman emperor Diocletian, was shot with arrows and was eventually drowned for his commitment to Christianity. While the arrow alludes to Saint Sebastian, the young man’s clothing dates to the late 1400s, indicating that this is a contemporary portrait, rather than an image of the historical saint. This haunting image was influenced by the paintings of Leonardo da Vinci (1452–1519), particularly in the artist’s use of smoky shadows (called sfumato) to model the flesh. It was painted by Marco d’Oggiono, a Milanese artist who worked in Leonardo’s studio.
cma:153406.title: Portrait of a Youth as Saint Sebastian

cma:153406.texto: While Marco d'Oggiono made numerous copies of the masterpieces of his teacher Leonardo da Vinci, this is an original composition.
cma:153406.title: Portrait of a Youth as Saint Sebastian

cma:97167.texto: Like other paintings from the Dossi workshop, this work conveys the sitter's social status and self-confidence. He holds a crumpled letter written in Italian. The words Asto, meaning "ship mast," and mare, meaning "sea," suggest that trade was a topic of this letter. References to anatomy and the word bella imply a discussion of the magnificence of human anatomy, an interest that spread rapidly during the Renaissance. The letter likewise communicates the young man's considerable education. This work was formerly called Portrait of Giuliano de Medici; however, the sitter's lack of resemblance to Giuliano caused art historians to discount this argument. Portrait of a Young Man was earlier attributed to Dosso's brother, Battista, before recently being considered a work by Dosso or a member of his workshop. As first suggested by Roberto Longhi, Portrait of a Young Man is now considered likely to be a work of an unidentified follower of Dossi from Friuli, Italy. The Friulian follower worked from 1510 until after 1530 and had connections to Dossi's hometown of Ferrara, accounting for this work's resemblance to Dossi's style. The dark outlines and large forms of the work are of a later style than Dossi's, suggesting that the artist was a follower rather than Dossi himself.
cma:97167.title: Portrait of a Young Man

formato.nota: El formato concreto **sigue abierto**: esto es la **cosmética declarada**, no el contrato. El contrato —`[n]` que asigna el renderizador, toda afirmación con dato citando un `fragment_id` recuperado en esta consulta, 100 % de los CC-BY con atribución, español + cita textual en inglés— vive en el código y es el conteo de referencias colgadas, el criterio de atribución, el criterio de idioma y las obligaciones de la cita.

salida.nota_de_idioma: el contrato de la salida citada / el criterio de idioma: la explicación en **español**, el fragmento citado **textual en inglés, sin traducir**. La cita viaja desde `knowledge` hasta acá **sin pasar por el modelo** (el contrato de salida), y las obligaciones de la cita lo verifica byte a byte: si el formateo viviera dentro del prompt, *'textual'* dependería de que el modelo no lo reescriba.

   El retrato fue realizado por Agnolo Bronzino, pintor de la corte de Cosimo I de’ Medici en Florencia, Italia. [1]
   La mujer retratada probablemente estaba afiliada a la corte Medici, lo que sugiere un retrato conmemorativo de una persona de alto estatus en Italia. [1]
   El retrato enfatiza la riqueza y el estatus social más que la expresión individual, característica común en retratos conmemorativos de la época.

   **Fuentes**
   [1] “Bronzino was court painter to Cosimo I de’Medici, the Duke of Florence. Though the woman cannot be definitively identified, she was likely affiliated with the Medici court. As in most of the portraits in this gallery, Bronzino emphasizes wealth, status, and courtly refinement above personality or individualized expression. The plain background further accentuates the work’s monumentality and grandeur, despite its small scale. The hand placed against the chest with elegantly spread fingers extends back to an ancient Greek pose of modesty, here emphasizing the proper comportment of a woman of high status. The sitter wears a linen partlet (collar) delicately embroidered in matt stitch, part of which is, like her cuffs, trimmed in fine lace.”
       https://clevelandart.org/art/1972.121 · CC0 1.0

3. **Portrait of a Woman**
   Andrea del Sarto · c. 1518 · oil on wood
   Ficha oficial: https://clevelandart.org/art/1944.92

   El retrato está vinculado a Andrea del Sarto, un pintor florentino, y fue realizado durante su estancia en Francia, pero la vestimenta del retratado es distintivamente francesa. [1]
   Aunque el artista es italiano, el retrato no corresponde a un contexto conmemorativo en Italia, sino en Francia.
   No hay suficiente información para afirmar que este retrato sea conmemorativo en Italia, dado que la vestimenta y contexto son franceses.

   **Fuentes**
   [1] “King Francis I’s deep interest in Italian Renaissance culture manifested itself not only through acquiring important works of art but also by bringing leading architects, scholars, and artists to Paris. Chief among these figures was the Florentine painter Andrea del Sarto. The sitter’s distinctively French hood and black veil suggest that someone talented closely connected to the artist painted this work during his brief time in France.”
       https://clevelandart.org/art/1944.92 · CC0 1.0

4. **Portrait of a Youth as Saint Sebastian**
   Marco d'Oggiono · late 1480s · oil on wood, transferred to pressed wood
   Ficha oficial: https://clevelandart.org/art/1986.9

   El retrato fue pintado por Marco d’Oggiono, un artista milanés que trabajó en el taller de Leonardo da Vinci, en Italia. [1]
   La imagen representa a un joven vestido con ropas del siglo XV, y no al santo histórico, sugiriendo un retrato contemporáneo con posible carácter conmemorativo. [1]
   El uso de técnicas leonardescas como el sfumato aporta un estilo refinado al retrato, típico de la pintura italiana renacentista.

   **Fuentes**
   [1] “Sebastian, a bodyguard for the ancient Roman emperor Diocletian, was shot with arrows and was eventually drowned for his commitment to Christianity. While the arrow alludes to Saint Sebastian, the young man’s clothing dates to the late 1400s, indicating that this is a contemporary portrait, rather than an image of the historical saint. This haunting image was influenced by the paintings of Leonardo da Vinci (1452–1519), particularly in the artist’s use of smoky shadows (called sfumato) to model the flesh. It was painted by Marco d’Oggiono, a Milanese artist who worked in Leonardo’s studio.”
       https://clevelandart.org/art/1986.9 · CC0 1.0

5. **Portrait of a Young Man**
   Dosso Dossi · c. 1530 · oil and gold on wood
   Ficha oficial: https://clevelandart.org/art/1916.803

   El retrato fue realizado por un seguidor de Dosso o de su taller, con conexiones a Ferrara, Italia. [1]
   El retrato comunica el estatus social y la educación del joven, lo que puede indicar un propósito conmemorativo.
   La obra fue atribuida inicialmente a Giuliano de Medici, aunque esta identificación fue descartada, pero mantiene su origen italiano. [1]

   **Fuentes**
   [1] “Like other paintings from the Dossi workshop, this work conveys the sitter's social status and self-confidence. He holds a crumpled letter written in Italian. The words Asto, meaning "ship mast," and mare, meaning "sea," suggest that trade was a topic of this letter. References to anatomy and the word bella imply a discussion of the magnificence of human anatomy, an interest that spread rapidly during the Renaissance. The letter likewise communicates the young man's considerable education. This work was formerly called Portrait of Giuliano de Medici; however, the sitter's lack of resemblance to Giuliano caused art historians to discount this argument. Portrait of a Young Man was earlier attributed to Dosso's brother, Battista, before recently being considered a work by Dosso or a member of his workshop. As first suggested by Roberto Longhi, Portrait of a Young Man is now considered likely to be a work of an unidentified follower of Dossi from Friuli, Italy. The Friulian follower worked from 1510 until after 1530 and had connections to Dossi's hometown of Ferrara, accounting for this work's resemblance to Dossi's style. The dark outlines and large forms of the work are of a later style than Dossi's, suggesting that the artist was a follower rather than Dossi himself.”
       https://clevelandart.org/art/1916.803 · CC0 1.0

nota_de_a8_vs_bd4: 🔴 **Las dos lecturas del libro mayor, y son proyecciones del mismo dato**: la tabla de costo pide el gasto *por etapa* y la atribución de cada llamada lo cuenta *por rol, no por el nombre de la etapa*. nota_de_identidad: Clase 2 (la tabla de identidades): *registro de una ejecución*. La identidad fija **las entradas, no la salida** —una salida no determinista con la misma entrada es el dato que el muestreo fijado, registrado y con su variabilidad medida mide—, así que lleva **ordinal** y la regla de que un id determina su contenido no aplica. El ordinal se **reserva** creando el directorio de forma exclusiva: `1 + n` es un *leer, después escribir* y el barrido es paralelo.
nota_de_la_tabla: degradación/la regla de qué corridas agregan a la tabla: una corrida con degradación **no planificada** no agrega a la tabla C0–C4 —*una C4 que degradó en silencio entraría etiquetada como C4 comportándose como C3*— y una con degradación **planificada** tampoco: es el criterio de respuesta garantizada y se reporta aparte. Una etapa **ausente por configuración** no degrada: no corre, y por eso C0–C3 sí agregan.

Un candidato **sin puntaje** degrada igual: ordenar mezclando «puntuado» con «no pude puntuarlo» sería publicar dos escalas en una columna, y los puntajes que sí se pagaron quedan en el artefacto.
